title: The LORD Is My Shepherd
summary: David pictures the LORD as a shepherd who provides pasture and water, restores his soul, and leads him in right paths for his name's sake. Even in the valley of the shadow of death he fears no evil, because God is with him. The image then shifts to a host who spreads a table in the presence of enemies, anoints his guest's head, and fills his cup, and the psalm ends with the confidence that goodness and mercy will follow him and he will dwell in the LORD's house forever.
story: Psalm 23 comes directly after Psalm 22, the cry of the forsaken sufferer whose praise ends with the poor eating and being satisfied. Here the sufferer's fear has been answered by presence: You are with me. It is the best-known psalm in the Bible, yet it is not naive; its peace is found in the valley and in the presence of enemies, not in their absence. It draws on the whole memory of Israel, whose God led them out of Egypt like a flock (Psalm 77:20), provided food and water in the wilderness, and brought them to rest in the land. And it looks forward to the prophets' promise that God himself would one day shepherd his scattered people (Ezekiel 34:11-16).
historical:
The superscription reads simply A Psalm of David. Traditional readers note that David was a shepherd before he was a king (1 Samuel 16:11, 17:34-35), and the psalm's images fit that background naturally. Many modern scholars read of David as marking a collection rather than authorship and date the psalm uncertainly; some think its references to the house of the LORD point to the temple, and so to a time after Solomon built it, while others note that the phrase was also used of the tabernacle (1 Samuel 1:7). No specific event is named, and the psalm has been prayed in every generation because it isn't tied to one.

The image of a king as a shepherd was common in the ancient Near East. Mesopotamian rulers used it of themselves; Hammurabi, the Babylonian king of the eighteenth century BC, calls himself a shepherd in the prologue to his law code. Israel used the image too, and God's charge to David was that he would shepherd God's people Israel (2 Samuel 5:2). Psalm 23 turns the royal image around: the king himself is a sheep, and the LORD is his shepherd.
cultural:
Shepherding in Judah was hard, dangerous work in dry country. Green pastures and quiet waters were not a lazy meadow but places a shepherd had to find and lead his flock toward, sometimes across long distances; sheep would not lie down unless they were fed and unafraid. The rod was a club for driving off predators, and the staff a longer stick for guiding and rescuing sheep. Paths of righteousness can mean right paths, tracks that lead where they should, rather than dead ends in the wilderness.

The second picture comes from the ancient code of hospitality. In the Near East a host who received a guest into his tent was bound to protect him, even from pursuers, for as long as he was under his roof. To spread a table in the presence of enemies is to receive a fugitive as an honored guest while those who want to harm him watch, unable to act. Anointing a guest's head with oil was a mark of welcome and honor (Luke 7:46), and an overflowing cup a sign of lavish generosity.
literary: The psalm is a psalm of trust, a type in which the whole prayer expresses confidence in God rather than complaint. It uses two main images, the shepherd (verses 1 to 4) and the host (verses 5 and 6), and some readers find a third, the guide on the road, in the paths and the valley. The grammar shifts meaningfully. In verses 1 to 3 the psalmist speaks about God in the third person (He makes me, He leads me). In verse 4, at the darkest point, he turns and speaks to God directly: for You are with me. That phrase sits near the center of the Hebrew poem. The last verse reverses the enemies' pursuit: goodness and mercy will follow, or pursue, him all his days.

outline.t: The shepherd who provides, restores, and leads
Through the dark valley: You are with me
The host who spreads a table before enemies
Goodness and mercy, and the house of the LORD forever

doctrines.note: God is pictured as a shepherd who provides, guides, protects, and restores. His care reaches through dark valleys, not only around them.
The psalm shows trust not as the absence of danger but as confidence in God's presence within it. Its heart is the simple confession, You are with me.
The goodness and mercy (chesed, covenant loyalty) that pursue the psalmist are God's steadfast love to his people. The shepherd's care is not sentiment but faithfulness to his own name.

words.note: Ra'ah, to shepherd, to pasture, to tend. The verb covers everything a shepherd does: feeding, leading, protecting, and rescuing. Kings were called shepherds of their people, and the prophets condemned Israel's leaders as shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock (Ezekiel 34:2). To say the LORD is my shepherd is to name God as the true king and caretaker.

Tsalmavet, traditionally the shadow of death. The word may be a compound of shadow and death, or it may be a word meaning deep darkness, from a root meaning to be dark. Either way it describes the darkest kind of place, a ravine where danger hides. The psalmist fears no evil there, not because it isn't dark but because God is with him.

Chesed, loving devotion, mercy, covenant love. It is the loyal love God has pledged to his people, love that holds when they have no claim on it. In verse 6 it is personified with goodness as a companion that follows, or pursues, the psalmist for the rest of his life.

Shuv, to return. In verse 6 the Hebrew text as vocalized reads I will return to the house of the LORD, while the ancient Greek and other versions read it as I will dwell, a form spelled almost the same. Most English translations choose dwell. Both readings end the psalm with the psalmist at home in God's presence.

christ: Jesus took up this psalm's central image and applied it to himself: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep” (John 10:11). In doing so he stepped into the role the Old Testament reserves for God himself (Ezekiel 34:15) and for the promised son of David whom God would set over his flock (Ezekiel 34:23). Hebrews calls Jesus that great Shepherd of the sheep, whom God brought back from the dead (Hebrews 13:20), and Peter calls him the Shepherd and Overseer of souls (1 Peter 2:25). The New Testament does not quote Psalm 23 directly, so the connection is through the shepherd theme that runs from the psalm through the prophets to Jesus. What it adds is striking: the shepherd who walks with his sheep through the valley of the shadow of death is the one who went into death for them.
questions: The psalmist says, “I shall not want.” What do you find yourself wanting most, and how does trusting God as shepherd speak to it?
The central confession comes in the darkest valley: for You are with me. When have you found God's presence most real in a hard place?
The table is spread in the presence of enemies, not after they are gone. What would it mean to receive God's care while your troubles are still in the room?
